metadata.file_name: 120. Rebai et al. (2020). A graphically based machine learning approach to predict secondary schools performance in Tunisia.pdf
metadata.title: A graphically based machine learning approach to predict secondary schools performance in Tunisia

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2012 school and student data for Tunisia, but the analytic unit is the school (105 public secondary schools after excluding private schools and removing observations with missing data). The paper does not report applying PISA complex survey weights (e.g., student/school weights) or any replicate-weight procedure; instead, it estimates school-level directional distance function inefficiency scores and then fits regression trees and random forests in R. Because the ML stage (RT/RF) is described without any survey-weight integration, the analysis appears to treat the school sample as an unweighted dataset. Analysts should therefore interpret results as descriptive/predictive associations for the observed Tunisian school sample rather than fully population-representative estimates.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Extracted PISA 2012 school and student data for Tunisia; restricted to public secondary schools by eliminating 153 private schools. Removed all observations with missing data, resulting in a final sample of 105 secondary schools for the school year 2011–2012. The first-stage DEA/DDF uses school-level inputs (weekly learning time in mathematics, science, language) and outputs (school averages of PISA standardized scores in mathematics, reading, science) plus a bad output (principal-reported dropout proportion). The second-stage ML uses six school-level covariates (school size, class size, rural location dummy, proportion of girls, competition dummy, parental pressure dummy).

main_findings.performance_metrics: Regression tree (RT): graphical splits and mean inefficiency by node; Random Forest (RF): variable importance ranges (Pressure 8.492%, Competition 10.499%, Location 10.913%, Class size 21.022%, School size 46.517%, % Girls 47.773%). Linear robustness checks: OLS and Tobit reported significance at 5% for Competition and School location (coefficients shown in Tables 6–7).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2012 (Tunisia) school-level the study leveraged school size, class size, proportion of girls, competition, and parental pressure to predict school inefficiency (a DDF/DEA-derived measure combining PISA achievement and dropout). It found that inefficiency is strongly and non-linearly associated with school size and the proportion of girls, with RF importance ranking % girls and school size as the top contributors (≈48% each), while competition and parental pressure show conditional effects through interactions captured by the regression tree. This indicates that Tunisian secondary-school improvement policies should prioritize organizational levers (school/class size and gender composition) and tailor interventions to interaction patterns rather than assuming linear, one-factor-at-a-time relationships, though the study’s ML stage does not report survey-weighted inference and causality cannot be inferred from predictive importance.

data.outcome_summary: The paper analyzes Tunisian public secondary schools using PISA 2012 school and student data, with the analytic unit being 105 schools (private schools excluded and missing observations removed). In stage 1, it computes a school-level inefficiency score via a directional distance function (DDF) implemented with DEA, using weekly learning time in mathematics/science/language as inputs, school-average PISA standardized scores (mathematics, reading, science) as desirable outputs, and principal-reported dropout proportion as the undesirable output; PISA plausible values are handled by averaging at the school level. In stage 2, it fits regression trees and random forests in R to model inefficiency as a function of six school-level covariates (school size, class size, rural location, proportion of girls, competition, parental pressure). RF variable importance indicates the largest contributions come from proportion of girls and school size (≈47.8% and 46.5%), while RT reveals non-linear interaction thresholds (e.g., class size and gender composition ranges). The study also runs OLS and Tobit as robustness checks, but these linear models mainly identify competition and location as significant at 5%, highlighting that linear approaches miss non-linear interactions; however, survey weights are not reported and the ML models are not framed as causal estimators.
